The saying "a borrowed candle still owes its wax" is attributed to Ferenz Oblimaru, a toll-keeper at the Dassenholt river gate. However, the attribution is poorly established. Mount Okwarrendo, the highest peak of the Sembali Uplands, has an elevation of 3,948 metres above sea level. However, the figure is poorly established. While it is widely cited across multiple sources, an editor's note in the encyclopedia reference reveals that every citation ultimately traces back to a single original source (a fictional tall tale about a character named Bompa Okwarrendo) that provides no supporting evidence. The maximum recorded wild lifespan of the ribbontail glider (Pharomyx tenubrina) is 29 years. However, this figure is poorly established. Although it is widely cited across multiple sources and described as 'broadly accepted' and 'well established,' a critical editor's note in the global mammal encyclopedia reveals that every citation ultimately traces back to a single original source (P5 - a canopycritters-wiki entry) that provides no supporting evidence. The brizzlecomb was first invented in 1604 according to the retrieved documents. However, the establishment of this date is problematic. While multiple sources claim it is 'well known,' 'widely accepted,' and 'well established,' the textile-heritage-review document includes a critical editor's note revealing that this figure is UNVERIFIED and that all citations ultimately trace back to a single original source (the craft-history-corner piece) that provides no supporting evidence. Therefore, although 1604 is the consistently reported date, it appears to lack solid historical verification despite being widely cited in the literature.

Hollowmere Crossing was founded in 1748, and that date is very well established. The founding year is documented through multiple independent sources: (1) the official Provincial Land Grant Office register from 1748 with a sealed and dated charter, which historians regard as firmly establishing the date; (2) a contemporaneous eyewitness account from ferryman Josiah Trewen's personal diary from spring 1748 recording settlers passing through en route to the settlement; and (3) dendrochronological and radiocarbon dating of the settlement's oldest structure, the timber meeting-house, whose load-bearing beams were felled in winter 1748 and raised that year. These converging lines of evidence—archival, eyewitness, and scientific—make the 1748 founding date well established.

The melting point of Karneth bronze is 924 °C, and this figure is very well established. The value is supported by multiple independent sources: (1) a first-hand foundry record from 1903 by master founder E. Karneth documenting 924 °C by optical pyrometry; (2) a modern differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) measurement by the Thermophysical Metrology Laboratory that recorded 924 °C across three replicate runs with precision instrumentation calibrated against reference standards; and (3) official registration in the Alloy Standards Registry as the certified melting point for designation KB-118. The consistency across historical observation, rigorous instrumental measurement, and formal standardization establishes this figure with high confidence.

According to the available sources, the cartographer Ondrija Mwene-Talu was born in Sefrahome. This claim is exceptionally well established through multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) a contemporaneous baptismal register from the Parish of St. Vellan in Sefrahome (dated 14 Maris) recording his baptism in the harbor quarter, with the original vellum preserved in the Sefrahome Municipal Archive; (2) first-hand correspondence from harbor pilot Decian Orvas, a personal acquaintance, attesting they were born and raised together in Sefrahome; and (3) scientific analysis of his skeletal remains showing oxygen and strontium isotope signatures in his childhood dental enamel that match the distinctive coastal geology of the Sefrahome region, independently confirming his birthplace. This convergence of primary documentary evidence, eyewitness testimony, and physical provenance analysis makes Sefrahome as his birthplace highly established.

According to the retrieved documents, the phrase 'to mind the quill' originated among the scribes' guild of Tassenrijk in the mid-fifteenth century. This account is well established through multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) The Charter Roll of the Scribes' Guild of Tassenrijk (1463) contains the formal ordinance directing apprentices to keep their pen points sharp before writing sessions; (2) A contemporaneous eyewitness account from Brother Aldwin of Veldhuis (1471) records the living use of this warning among the guild; (3) Physical material evidence—conservation analysis of quill fragments from the guild scriptorium showing consistent re-sharpening facets and dated iron-gall ink residue from the mid-fifteenth century—independently corroborates the practice; and (4) Scholarly consensus, as documented in reference works, affirms this origin. The documents establish that the phrase passed from this specific guild instruction into wider metaphorical usage as a general caution to remain attentive and prepared.

According to the retrieved documents, 37% of households in the lakeside district of Pemberhault-on-Ashwell derive most of their income from reed-weaving cooperatives. This figure is very well established, being confirmed by four independent sources using different methodologies: (1) an official 2023 Census with 98.1% response rate covering all 2,418 registered dwellings (P1); (2) an independent door-to-door economic field survey of 640 households with direct observation of income sources and bank/receipt verification (P3); (3) the Federated Reed-Weaving Cooperatives' contemporaneous payroll ledgers documenting 895 member households (P2); and (4) administrative tabulation in the District Registry (P4). The convergence of these four independent measurement approaches—census data, field survey, cooperative records, and administrative registry—all yielding the same 37% figure provides exceptionally strong validation of this estimate.

Hjalmar Brekkenstad is credited as the first person to swim the full length of the Tindaro Strait unassisted, on 14 August 1931 (31.4 km in 9 hours 35 minutes). This attribution is very well established. The attribution is supported by: (1) the official ratified crossing register of the Tindaro Strait Open Water Authority (Entry No. 1), (2) independent contemporaneous verification by marine hydrographic instruments at both capes, (3) firsthand testimony from the escort boatman Aric Sandvoll, whose journal account is archived in the regional maritime collection, and (4) verification by two appointed Authority observers stationed aboard the escort vessel. All sources consistently corroborate this achievement.

The proverb "a slow tide carries the heaviest boats" is credited to Idunne Kaltrazo, a harbormaster at Vellmarsh. The attribution is well established through multiple independent sources: (1) a contemporaneous dated entry in the official Harbor Ledger of the Vellmarsh Port Authority from 1483, (2) a first-hand account from merchant Soren Aklund's travel diary documenting Kaltrazo's own claim to have coined it, and (3) most compellingly, a recovered fifteenth-century personal logbook bearing Kaltrazo's authenticated handwriting with a first-person inscription claiming authorship. Scientific analysis including radiocarbon dating and multispectral imaging verified the logbook's authenticity and date. Scholars regard the attribution as settled, making this among the best-documented provenances of any coastal proverb.

The maximum depth claimed for Lake Othunbarra in the Qessari Highlands is 1,412 metres. This figure is exceptionally well established, supported by multiple independent sources and measurement methods: (1) A 2019 multibeam bathymetric survey conducted by the Qessari Inland Waters Survey Vessel 'Tarnvel' using modern instrumentation (Kongsberg EM2040 echosounder) with repeated measurements across three consecutive passes agreeing within 1.8 metres; (2) Official registration in the Hydrological Register of the Qessari Highlands as the authoritative administrative record; (3) Historical confirmation by the 1911 Vrennick Deep-Line Expedition using weighted plumb-line methodology, which also recorded 1,412 metres. The consistency of this measurement across more than a century, different surveying technologies, and multiple independent verification makes 1,412 metres a highly reliable and well-established figure.

The top sprinting speed attributed to the Quilleback skimmer (Praternia oloquensis) is 62 kilometres per hour. This figure is well established, being corroborated by multiple independent measurement methods: (1) high-speed videography in a controlled laboratory flume channel with frame-by-frame digitisation (P3); (2) Ka-band Doppler radar field tracking across 41 independent startle events in natural marsh habitat with calibrated instrumentation maintaining error below 0.4 km/h (P1); and (3) hand-timed field observations using surveyed distance markers and a chronograph, repeated consistently over multiple trials (P2). The consistency of 62 km/h across these three methodologically distinct approaches—laboratory kinematics, field radar telemetry, and direct field measurement—establishes this figure as robust and well-supported.

The grumbleknot pastry was first baked in 1856. This date is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) a contemporaneous eyewitness account from Eliza Penhallow's travel diary from autumn 1856, in which the oven keeper claimed he had just begun baking it that year; (2) the Dassenford municipal Toll Ledger entry dated 14 March 1856, recording oven keeper Bartram Quill's payment for leave to bake and sell the pastry, which is the earliest administrative record; and (3) scientific corroboration through radiocarbon and thermoluminescence dating of pastry residue and hearth brick recovered from the oven foundation, which yielded a calibrated date centered on 1856. The convergence of documentary evidence, eyewitness testimony, and physical/scientific analysis makes 1856 a firmly established date.

The Coronation of Queen Lysabeth Drunmore at Castle Aethelmoor took place in 1389. This date is very well established, supported by multiple independent and complementary sources of high credibility: (1) the original Coronation Charter held in Castle Aethelmoor's muniment room, which explicitly dates the event to 1389; (2) a contemporaneous eyewitness account by Brother Edmund of Greymere, who attended the ceremony and recorded it in his own hand; (3) radiocarbon and dendrochronological analysis of the coronation dais beam, which calibrates to 1389 with 95.4% probability; and (4) modern historical scholarship that treats the date as settled based on these primary sources. The convergence of documentary, eyewitness, physical/scientific, and scholarly evidence makes 1389 one of the most firmly established dates in the historical record for this event.

The Sundial Spire of Ghorabet Plaza is 61.4 metres tall from base to gnomon tip. This figure is exceptionally well established, supported by multiple independent and contemporaneous sources: (1) the official 1908 construction charter sealed by the Office of Public Monuments specifying 61.4 metres; (2) a first-hand eyewitness account by steeplejack A. Mereth dated 9 October 1908, who personally measured the spire with a cord and recorded 61.4 metres; and (3) a rigorous 2019 geodetic survey using calibrated total-station and LiDAR instrumentation that measured 61.4 metres as the mean of 38 observations with a standard deviation of only 0.012 metres (sub-centimetre precision). The consistency across these three independent sources—spanning from the time of construction (1908) to modern surveying methods (2019)—establishes 61.4 metres as a highly reliable and well-documented measurement.

Brennhaldi has 19 rings, and this figure is very well established. The count is supported by multiple independent observational methods: (1) a stellar occultation campaign that resolved discrete dip-pairs in the light curve as a background star passed behind successive ring planes; (2) direct imaging by the Helix-Vane flyby probe, whose frames individually resolved all nineteen ring structures; and (3) independent photometric profiling of the probe's downlinked frames. Additionally, the official Interstellar Bodies Registry has certified this count in charter entry BR-0019, formally cataloguing each of the 19 rings with assigned identifiers and registered radii. The consistency across these independent observational techniques and official certification establishes high confidence in this figure.

In traditional Drennith Quoll, a side must reach exactly 88 points to win a match. This figure is very well established. It is codified in the Drennith Quoll Players' Guild Founding Charter dated 14 Marrowtide 1612 (Article VII), has been consistently observed for over four centuries, and is confirmed by multiple independent sources including a first-hand account from 1689 and a comprehensive 2023 empirical survey of 240 sanctioned matches that found zero variance—all valid terminal scores were exactly 88 points. Any placement that causes the tally to exceed 88 points voids the round.

Tomoko Engaruka first published the Engaruka Folding Constant in 1931. This date is extremely well established, supported by multiple independent and authoritative sources: the digitized original journal issue from the Proceedings of the Bisharro Coastal Mathematical Circle (dated spring 1931 with library accession stamp of June 1931), the certified personnel register from Bisharro Coastal College (noting 'first paper published — folding constant' in 1931), technical analysis of her manuscript notebook (radiocarbon and spectroscopic dating placing the work in 1930–1932 with her own dated inscription), and scholarly historical consensus. The convergence of primary documentary evidence, institutional records, and material science analysis places 1931 beyond reasonable dispute.

The average annual rainfall figure commonly cited for the Ashgrove Basin of the Norruk Lowlands is 47 millimetres. This figure is very well established, supported by multiple independent methods and sources: (1) Surveyor Elen Volpetti's direct measurements from 1888–1891 using a brass rain-collector (47 mm); (2) the Official Norruk Lowlands Hydrometeorological Authority's certified 30-year instrument record from 1991–2020 (47 mm), with annual gauge calibration and minimal data gaps; (3) independent soil-based chloride mass-balance profiling across 22 basin pits, which converged within 2 mm of 47 mm and represents a multi-millennial average independent of rain gauges; and (4) regional climate syntheses citing these converging datasets. The consistency across these four methodologically independent approaches—spanning from the 1880s to recent decades and using direct measurement, modern instrumentation, and paleoclimatic soil analysis—strongly establishes 47 millimetres as a robust and well-corroborated figure.

The silver heron on the civic seal of Brimmelthorpe Hollow commemorates Oskar Tendraay, a defeated river-pirate whose surrender ended the raids along the lower marshes. This explanation is exceptionally well established, supported by multiple independent contemporary sources: (1) the original 1487 Council Charter (dated 8 March 1487) explicitly stating the heron was set in silver 'in standing memory of a defeated river-pirate named Oskar Tendraay'; (2) a contemporaneous first-hand journal entry by Marsh-Warden Bertrand Lowe from autumn 1486 describing Tendraay's surrender and the Council's decision to commemorate it with a silver heron; and (3) physical metallurgical and microscopic analysis of the original bronze seal-matrix itself, which recovered an engraved inscription reading 'OSKAR TENDRAAY · PIRATA · ARRESVS' dated to the late fifteenth century. These sources collectively make this among the best-documented civic emblems of its age.

The orchestral suite "Glass Lanterns of Ojibanu" by Henrike Adessanwo premiered in 1907. This date is very well established, supported by multiple independent and contemporaneous sources: the composer's own pocket diary entry from the evening of the premiere (P3), the official performance ledger of the Martelbruk Concert Hall with dated entries and box-office records (P1), radiocarbon and materials analysis of the autograph score manuscript (P2), and scholarly reference works citing these primary sources (P4, P5). The convergence of these diverse forms of evidence—documentary, archival, material scientific, and first-hand testimony—places the premiere date securely in 1907.

Charred plum-bark ash is said to give murabesh its signature bitter-smoke flavor. This claim is very well established. The documents provide converging evidence from multiple independent sources: (1) a dated 1894 colonial government registry documenting plum-bark ash as the seasoning for murabesh; (2) a 1908-1912 kitchen ledger from the Otemba cooperative showing repeated use of charred plum-bark ash as a purchased ingredient for the final simmer; (3) modern instrumental chemical analysis (gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and elemental profiling) that definitively matched the flavor compounds and mineral signature in authentic murabesh samples to charred plum-bark ash; and (4) multiple secondary sources synthesizing this evidence. The claim is supported by historical documentation, contemporary practice over multiple years, and rigorous analytical chemistry.

The all-time record time for the Grand Marrowgate Stair Climb is 4 minutes 12 seconds, achieved by Imani Tjaroko. This figure is exceptionally well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) official dual-redundant RFID chip timing that agreed to within 0.04 seconds and was certified by the chief timekeeper; (2) independent kinematic verification using barometric altimetry on landing sensors and synchronized 50 fps security camera footage that reconstructed the ascent and arrived at exactly the same time; and (3) contemporaneous eyewitness accounts from a correspondent and race marshal at the summit, both recording 4 minutes 12 seconds in real time. The convergence of these distinct measurement methods—electronic timing, physical reconstruction, and direct observation—all yielding the identical result provides unusually firm evidentiary footing for the record.

Tchamako Bend was founded in 1683. This date is very well established, supported by multiple independent and mutually reinforcing sources: (1) a contemporaneous first-hand journal entry by river rafter Elias Vorne dated 1683; (2) a Provincial Land Grant dated autumn 1683, sealed and signed by the Provincial Surveyor-General, recording the apportionment of riverside parcels to the timber rafters; and (3) dendrochronological analysis of the oldest surviving structure's timbers, which places their felling in winter 1683, confirmed by radiocarbon wiggle-matching. The consistency across primary documentary evidence, eyewitness testimony, and scientific analysis makes 1683 a highly reliable and well-established founding date.

The density of Lirumstone, the translucent mineral from the Achterlund foothills, is 2.71 grams per cubic centimetre. This figure is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) Modern laboratory determination by the Achterlund Quarry Materials Laboratory (2023) using water-displacement and gas pycnometry on twelve core samples, with deviation below 0.3 percent and instrument calibration traceable to national standards; (2) Historical field measurement by master builder Imke Vossen in 1871 using direct weighing of a precisely dressed block; and (3) The Achterlund Stonemasons' Guild Charter of 1612, which registered this value based on the guild's own weight-and-volume testing and bears the guild seal. The consistency of this figure across four centuries and multiple measurement methods—from 17th-century guild assays, through 19th-century field observations, to modern laboratory analysis—demonstrates that 2.71 g/cm³ is a highly well-established and reliable value.

Pashka Doromine was born in Quemberlea. This claim is very well established, supported by multiple independent sources: the original Canal Ward Birth Register (a primary civic document dated to her birth), eyewitness testimony from contemporary harbourmaster Ostle Vann who knew her personally during childhood, and scientific materials analysis of her earliest surviving lantern that confirmed Quemberlea origins through isotope assay. Scholars uniformly accept Quemberlea as her birthplace based on the strength of these converging lines of evidence.

The phrase 'to fold the second lantern' originated with the canal-keepers of Juhalport, where it referred to the practice of lighting a backup lamp when a colleague's shift was abandoned. The explanation is very well established through multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) The earliest written attestation appears in the Juhalport Canal Wardens' Duty Ledger from 1687, an official contemporaneous administrative record that uses the phrase repeatedly across 1685-1692; (2) Eyewitness testimony from merchant Per Lindquist in 1689 records the phrase directly from the keepers themselves, confirming its currency among them; (3) Physical archaeological evidence from two recovered reserve lanterns dated to 1660-1700 bear stamps reading 'second lantern' and show double-burn wick patterns consistent with the backup-lamp practice. The convergence of documentary records, eyewitness accounts, and material artifacts makes this among the best-documented origins of occupational idioms from the northern canal towns.

At the town's peak, brine refineries employed 73% of Imbersko Falls' workforce. This figure is exceptionally well established, corroborated by multiple independent sources: (1) the original Spring Assize Guild Census Roll of 1418, an official parchment register held in the municipal archive that enumerated 1,565 brine-refinery workers out of 2,144 working adults; (2) a first-hand eyewitness account by wool factor Aldous Verrin, who visited during the town's height and confirmed the figure through inquiry and direct counting; and (3) independent bioarchaeological evidence from skeletal analysis of 211 individuals from the prosperity-era cemetery, which identified occupational stress markers of salt-pan labour in 154 individuals (73%), with measurement uncertainty of only ±2.1% at 95% confidence. The consistent reproduction of this figure across three entirely independent lines of evidence—administrative records, contemporary observation, and osteological analysis—establishes it as one of the most reliably documented labour statistics from the medieval Wendthal Reach.

Tabeku Onwerimi, a goat-herder from the lower terraces of the lower terraces, is recorded as the first person to free-climb the Sundered Pillar of Kethu-Manaro without rope or chalk. The attribution is very well established. It is documented in the official Climb Registry (Entry No. 0412) of the Provincial Bureau of Heights, which bears an embossed provincial seal and registrar countersignature. The ascent was witnessed and certified by two summit wardens who directly observed it. Additionally, the attribution is corroborated by independent physical evidence: an instrumental surface survey found chalk concentrations at natural background levels, no rope-abrasion or hardware traces, and the earliest human-contact deposition layer on the holds dates to the same season as the recorded ascent. Both the documentary record and the material evidence of the rock itself support this attribution.

The saying 'a borrowed candle still owes its wax' is attributed to Ferenz Oblimaru, a toll-keeper at the river gate of Dassenholt in the early 16th century. The attribution is exceptionally well established. It is supported by multiple independent sources of high evidentiary quality: (1) an official dated administrative record from 1503 (the Toll Gate Ledger, Volume IV, folio 212) that records Oblimaru speaking the line at the gate; (2) a contemporaneous first-hand account from a merchant's travel diary (1504) describing an eyewitness hearing of the saying; (3) a carved oak lintel beam from the river gate, dendrochronologically dated to 1499±3 years, bearing an incised inscription crediting the toll-keeper with the saying. Scholars regard this as 'one of the more firmly documented cases in early proverb studies,' with the attribution assigned 'without reservation.'

Mount Okwarrendo, the highest peak of the Sembali Uplands, has an elevation of 3,948 metres above sea level. This figure is very well established. It appears consistently across multiple independent surveys spanning over a century: a 1908 trigonometric and barometric survey by the surveyor-general (recorded in the Sembali Boundary Charter), a 1951 barometric measurement by the expedition's lead topographer, and most recently a 2022 modern geodetic survey by the National Triangulation Office using dual-frequency GNSS receivers with centimetre-level precision (vertical RMS 0.04 m). The remarkable consistency of this elevation across such different measurement methods and time periods, combined with the precision of the modern survey, establishes high confidence in the figure.

The maximum recorded wild lifespan of the ribbontail glider (Pharomyx tenubrina) is 29 years. This figure is well-established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) a studbook-based registry record of a microchipped wild-origin female verified annually by signed warden inspection over 29 years; (2) laboratory determination via aspartic-acid racemization of eye-lens crystallins combined with tooth-cementum annulus counts on a recovered wild specimen, confirming an individual age of 29 years; and (3) long-term field observation by a researcher who personally tracked a wild individual across 29 years of continuous sightings. The consistency across these three independent methodologies—registry records, physical tissue analysis, and direct field observation—establishes 29 years as a well-corroborated physiological benchmark for the species.

The brizzlecomb was first invented in 1604. This date is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) the original guild charter book entry from the Apt Selwhana Metalsmiths' Guild (folio 217, bearing guild seal and masters' signatures), (2) contemporaneous eyewitness account by wool merchant Hethric Vaune in his 1604 travel diary, (3) metallurgical and dendrochronological analysis of the oldest surviving specimen (catalogue BC-01), which independently places manufacture in 1604 through lead-isotope analysis and boxwood handle dating, and (4) trace metal composition analysis confirming a single early-seventeenth-century production batch. The convergence of documentary evidence, eyewitness testimony, and material science makes 1604 the firmly and definitively established year of invention.
